findings.finding: The new per-account login limiter added for QA-AUTH-001 (20 attempts/hour, keyed on email only) is never reset on a successful login — only the per-IP counter is cleared — and the application exposes no admin-facing way to clear a tripped RateLimit row. A legitimately busy account (shared helpdesk/coordinator login, multiple devices, a password manager retrying a stale credential, or simply 20 successful same-hour logins) is locked out of every subsequent login attempt for up to 60 minutes with no in-app remedy other than waiting out the window.
evidence: src/auth.ts:36-41 — accountLimiterKey is charged by every authorize() call, success or failure, via Promise.all before credentials are even checked

src/auth.ts:47-49 — comment confirms the design choice: 'Only the per-IP counter is cleared on success. Clearing the account counter too would let one correct password reset the budget for an ongoing spray against the same account.'
src/lib/rate-limit.ts:46-49 — resetRateLimit() exists but is called nowhere for the account-keyed bucket, and no admin action in src/server/actions anywhere calls it

src/auth.ts:41 — if (!limit.success || !accountLimit.success) return null; — identical to the invalid-credentials path, so a locked-out legitimate user sees the same generic failure already filed as QA-AUTH-004, with no indication that waiting (rather than resetting a password) is the fix
reproduction: Not reproduced — no database is available in this run to drive 21 authorize() calls against one account and observe the lockout

Derived from static reading of src/auth.ts and src/lib/rate-limit.ts: every call to authorize() increments the account-keyed row regardless of outcome, and nothing in the codebase ever deletes or resets that row before its one-hour expiry
findings.expected: A rate limiter wide enough not to be casually self-triggered by legitimate use, or an operator-facing way to clear it when it is
findings.actual: No reset path exists for the account-keyed bucket under any circumstance short of the hour elapsing, and the fix's own code comment shows this was a deliberate trade-off that the fix_applied description does not surface as a residual risk
findings.root_cause: QA-AUTH-001 was fixed by adding a wider-window per-account counter that is intentionally harder to reset than the per-IP one, to close the IP-rotation gap the finding described — but no corresponding operator override was added
findings.uncertainty: Whether any real account plausibly makes 20+ login attempts (successful or not) within a rolling hour was not verified — this depends on usage patterns not observable from code. Confirm by checking login telemetry/ActivityLog LOGIN counts per user per hour once a database is available, or by adding an admin action that calls resetRateLimit('login:account:' + hashIdentifier(email))
findings.user_impact: If triggered, a legitimate user is fully locked out of the application for up to an hour with a message indistinguishable from 'wrong password' (QA-AUTH-004), and no administrator action exists to shorten that wait
findings.recommendation: Add an admin action (ADMIN role only) that clears a specific account's login rate-limit keys, for use when a legitimate lockout is reported, and surface a distinct 'too many attempts, try again at HH:MM' message (QA-AUTH-004) so the user knows waiting is the correct action rather than resetting their password
regression_coverage: Mechanical: typecheck PASS, lint PASS, test:unit 19/19 PASS (none of the 19 tests exercise src/auth.ts or src/lib/rate-limit.ts)
Still needed: an integration test driving 21 authorize() calls for one account and asserting both the lockout and the absence of any reset path (requires a database)

findings.finding: qa/reports/diff-scope.json's top-level `changed` array and `counts.changedFiles` (6) omit src/app/api/club/documents/[id]/file/route.ts, even though that file is part of the actual 7-file change set for this regression pass (it carries the QA-API-001 fix) and its downstream route (`api.club.documentFile`) does appear inside `impact.downstreamNodes` and `impact.routes`.
evidence: qa/reports/diff-scope.json:5-12 — `changed` lists exactly 6 files; src/app/api/club/documents/[id]/file/route.ts is not among them

qa/reports/diff-scope.json:87 and :136 — `impact.routes` and `impact.downstreamNodes` both independently reference the club-documents file route and `api.club.documentFile`, so the omission did not create a blind spot in this pass, but the file list itself is stale relative to the 7-file change set given in this task's brief
reproduction: Compare the CHANGE SET in the task brief (7 files) against qa/reports/diff-scope.json's `changed` array (6 files) and `counts.changedFiles` (6)
findings.expected: diff-scope.json's file list and count match the actual set of files modified for the approved fixes it is meant to scope
findings.actual: The scope file undercounts by one file. In this instance the downstream graph walk happened to already include the missing file's route (likely because another seed file shares a dependency with it), so no impacted node was missed — but a future run that trusts `changed`/`counts.changedFiles` as the authoritative file list, rather than re-deriving it, could silently skip impact analysis for a file left out this way
findings.root_cause: diff-scope.json appears to have been generated before the QA-API-001 fix (club-documents route) was applied, or that file was added to the change set after the scope script ran, and the script was not re-run
findings.user_impact: None at runtime. A process gap that could cause a future regression pass to under-scope its impact analysis
findings.recommendation: Re-run scripts/scope-diff.mjs against the full, final 7-file change set before closing this regression cycle, so `changed` and `counts.changedFiles` are accurate for any later audit of this run
